name: Tauranga
title: Tauranga Hull Gauging: UTM for Log Carriers, Reefers & Tankers
description: Thickness gauging in Tauranga at Mount Maunganui and Sulphur Point for log carriers, container ships, reefers and tankers: holds, hatch covers and tanks.
h1: Ship Thickness Measurement at the Port of Tauranga and Mount Maunganui
intro: Tauranga, on the Bay of Plenty, is New Zealand's busiest port by cargo volume, exporting logs, kiwifruit and dairy produce and handling the country's largest container flows across two wharf areas on either side of the harbour. Log carriers loading at Mount Maunganui and reefer ships in the fruit season generate much of the gauging work. Atlantis has nobody based in New Zealand: technicians are flown in from India for each ship once the visa and the berth window are settled.
keywords: ballast tank gauging bay of plenty

highlights.h: Log carriers and their hard-worked holds
highlights.p: Handysize bulk carriers fitted with log stanchions load radiata pine at Mount Maunganui for Asian sawmills. Log hooks, grabs and heavy deck stows batter hatch coamings, hold frames and stanchion sockets, so hold and coaming gauging with crack detection at bracket toes is a frequent request here.

highlights.h: Reefer and container calls in fruit season
highlights.p: The kiwifruit harvest fills Tauranga with reefer ships and extra container calls from autumn onwards. Refrigerated holds and their insulation hide the steel, so owners often use a stay alongside to gauge ballast tanks, decks and piping that can be reached without disturbing the cargo spaces.

highlights.h: Hoist and hardstand at Sulphur Point
highlights.p: The council-owned marine precinct at Sulphur Point runs New Zealand's largest vessel hoist, lifting fishing boats, workboats and large yachts onto hardstand. Hulls out of the water there can be gauged from outside, with internal tanks and voids measured during the same visit.

port.h: Harbour entrance, two wharf areas and the Bay of Plenty anchorage
p: Tauranga Harbour is a long, shallow tidal lagoon sheltered behind Matakana Island, and ships enter through a narrow channel that runs close beneath Mauao, the volcanic cone at the tip of the Mount Maunganui peninsula. Strong tidal streams sweep the entrance, so movements of the largest ships are planned around tide and current windows, with compulsory pilotage and tug escort. The channel and berth pockets were deepened in the last decade to admit bigger container ships. Inside, the port divides in two: the Mount Maunganui wharves on the eastern shore, a long continuous quay backed by storage land, cool stores and a separate tanker berth to the south, and the Sulphur Point container terminal on the western side, facing the city across the water. Ships arriving ahead of their window wait offshore in the open Bay of Plenty.

Exports dominate. Logs from the central North Island's plantation forests arrive by road and rail and are loaded at Mount Maunganui onto log carriers bound mainly for China, with India and other Asian buyers taking smaller volumes. Kiwifruit leaves in reefer ships and refrigerated containers through the harvest and storage season, and dairy produce, meat and timber products move in containers through Sulphur Point. Imports include fertiliser and its raw materials, cement and stock feed, and the tanker berth handles petroleum products, chemicals and edible oils. Cruise ships use the Mount Maunganui wharves through the southern summer, and the port also sees coastal ships, fishing vessels, tugs and dredgers. Bunker points along the Mount Maunganui quay let ships refuel while they work cargo, a convenience that shapes how a ship's crew is deployed during a call.

Seasons shape the work. The kiwifruit export season builds from autumn and runs into winter, bringing reefer ships, extra container services and pressure on berths, while log exports follow demand in China and can rise or fall sharply from month to month. During periods of congestion in recent years, ships have queued in the Bay of Plenty for days waiting to berth, which gives an owner time for tank work if the weather offshore allows launch transfers. Summer brings the cruise ships, sometimes more than one in a day, and fills the Mount Maunganui berths. The Bay is open to the north and north-east, so a swell or a strong onshore wind can stop boat transfers even when the harbour itself is calm.

facilities.h: Where a ship can be gauged in Tauranga
p: Alongside work is the norm. At the Mount Maunganui wharves the team boards log carriers, bulk carriers, reefers and general cargo ships during loading or discharge, working holds while they are empty and moving to ballast tanks and deck structure while cargo work continues. The tanker berth to the south takes product, chemical and edible-oil tankers under the terminal's own permit rules, which govern what can be opened and when. At Sulphur Point, container ships give a shorter window, normally used for deck plating, hatch coamings, lashing bridges and selected tanks. Because ships often refuel alongside, tank entry is planned around the fuel transfer and the deck crew's availability rather than squeezed in against it.

There is no dry dock in Tauranga able to take a merchant ship. The Sulphur Point marine precinct, owned by Tauranga City Council and run under its Vessel Works name, lifts fishing vessels, workboats and large yachts with the country's largest vessel hoist and places them on hardstand for refit, a good setting for complete hull gauging of small craft. Larger ships needing a dry dock go to Auckland's Calliope Dock if they fit, to Lyttelton's dock for smaller vessels, or more often to yards in Asia, so the Tauranga call becomes the place to measure steel before the docking.

Tanker berth south of the Mount Maunganui wharves — product, chemical and edible-oil tankers under the terminal's permit system
Sulphur Point container terminal — deck, hatch coaming and tank readings on container ships during their exchange
Bay of Plenty anchorage — tank work during a berth wait when the weather allows launch transfers
Sulphur Point marine precinct — fishing vessels, workboats and large yachts lifted onto hardstand by the vessel hoist
Cruise berths at Mount Maunganui — piping and technical spaces on summer cruise calls

context.h: Port state control, biosecurity and the log trade at Tauranga
p: Maritime New Zealand carries out port state control at Tauranga under the Tokyo MoU, and the port's heavy bulk and log trade brings older handysize bulk carriers in front of its inspectors more often than at most New Zealand ports. The grounding of the container ship Rena on Astrolabe Reef off Tauranga in 2011 is still remembered as the country's worst maritime environmental disaster, and it keeps structural condition and safe navigation in sharp focus on this coast. Biosecurity is administered by the Ministry for Primary Industries, and log exports carry their own phytosanitary requirements: logs are treated against pests on the wharf or fumigated in the hold after loading, and fumigation decides when anyone can safely enter a loaded hold.

The log trade is hard on ships. Logs are lifted aboard with hooks and chains, stowed high on deck between stanchions and lashed down for the crossing to Asia, so hatch covers carry heavy point loads and coaming tops, stanchion sockets and lashing points take repeated knocks. Bark and wood debris clog hold drains and bilge wells, holding moisture against the tank top and frame feet. On other voyages the same ships often carry steel, fertiliser or grain, adding abrasion and chemical attack. Reefer ships bring a different set of problems: their cold, insulated holds stay dry inside, but condensation forms where chilled steel meets warm air, in ballast tanks, on deckheads and around hatch coamings, and that is where corrosion builds up out of sight.

jobs.h: Gauging jobs we see at Tauranga
jobs.p: Most Tauranga requests come from owners and managers of log and bulk carriers, reefers and container ships that dock elsewhere, and from buyers inspecting ships before sale. The work is fitted around loading and the tide-governed movements in the entrance channel, so the agent's berth plan sets the window and the scope is ranked to fit it. Holds are gauged on arrival, empty and in ballast, before the first logs go in, and ballast tanks are opened as the ship's ballast plan allows. On log carriers, hatch cover tightness testing and crack detection at coaming corners often go with the gauging, because water through a leaking cover can ruin a fertiliser or grain cargo on a later voyage.
list: Hold, hatch coaming and stanchion socket gauging on a handysize log carrier before loading at Mount Maunganui, with magnetic particle crack detection at bracket toes and coaming corners.
Ultrasonic hatch cover tightness test and coaming gauging on a log carrier that will load a dry bulk cargo on its next voyage.
Owner's condition gauging of a reefer ship's ballast tanks, deckheads and coamings during a kiwifruit loading call.
Pre-docking steel estimate on a container ship at Sulphur Point before its renewal survey in an Asian yard.
Pre-purchase inspection of a product tanker at the tanker berth, sampling deck plating, ballast tanks and cargo piping for a buyer.
Hull gauging of a fishing vessel or workboat on the hardstand at the Sulphur Point marine precinct.

logistics: Tauranga Airport has domestic flights only, so the team flies into Auckland International Airport and continues to the Bay of Plenty by a short domestic connection or by road. Indian nationals need a New Zealand visa suited to short-term specialist work, applied for once the ship's call is firm and supported by a letter describing the job; processing times vary, so early notice helps. The ship's agent arranges port inductions and escorted access to the wharves, and the marine precinct's own site rules apply to vessels on the hardstand.
vessels: Handysize log carriers and bulk carriers

faqs.q: Can a log carrier's holds be gauged at Mount Maunganui?
faqs.a: Yes, ideally on arrival, when the ship comes in empty from its last discharge port and before the first logs are loaded. Holds need to be dry, lit and ventilated, with safe access to frames, brackets and the tank top. Once loading starts the holds fill quickly, so we agree the order of holds with the chief officer and work one hold ahead of the loading sequence where the plan allows.

faqs.q: Does log fumigation affect an inspection in Tauranga?
faqs.a: It can. Logs are treated against pests either on the wharf or in the hold after loading, and a hold under fumigation cannot be entered until it has been ventilated and cleared by the fumigation contractor. Hold work is therefore scheduled before treatment, while deck, hatch cover and ballast tank work can carry on around it. The ship's agent confirms the fumigation plan when the call is booked.

faqs.q: Is there a dry dock in Tauranga?
faqs.a: Not for merchant ships. The Sulphur Point marine precinct lifts fishing vessels, workboats and yachts onto hardstand with its vessel hoist, and those can be gauged out of the water. Bulk carriers, reefers and container ships calling here dock in Asia or elsewhere, so a Tauranga call is the place to collect steel data for the yard before the ship sails north.

faqs.q: Can tank work be done while a ship waits in the Bay of Plenty?
faqs.a: When the weather allows. The anchorage is in open water, and a north-easterly swell can stop launch transfers for a day or more. If a ship is expected to wait, we plan ballast tank and void work for the anchorage, keep a ranked list, and move any unfinished compartments to the berth. The agent books the launch and confirms the boarding window with the master.

faqs.q: What are the busiest times of year at Tauranga?
faqs.a: The kiwifruit season, from autumn into winter, adds reefer ships and container calls, and the cruise season fills the Mount Maunganui berths in summer. Log exports vary with demand from China rather than with the calendar. Busy periods mean tighter berth windows, so we confirm the ship's slot with the agent early and prepare a shorter, ranked scope if the stay is likely to be brief.
